I am Hester Vance. I am past retirement age, which means I have nothing now but time and memory. The marker stands in my mind as clear as it stood in that field sixty years ago. I have been waiting.

There is a conversation begun here at home with Rosalind, only two turns gone. I know what I came here to do.

My daughter Rosalind has the mill, runs it with her hands and will not let anyone else touch the books. My other daughter Ainsley married the quarry, or the money that came with it. I worry about the wrong one. I always have. But this morning I am thinking of what must be said while I can still say it.

I was standing right there. When your father was alive—when he was still walking beside me—we watched them move it. The elm came later. Idris Thorne was a boy then, barely knee-high, and he is repeating what his father told him, the same as his father repeated lies. The marker was at the bent hawthorn. I saw it. I was standing right there.

Junia speaks of borders and papers, of Kem Okonjo waiting to see if she will transfer something. My granddaughter has always been the one who counts. I have caught her staring at the mill accounts when she thought herself alone. She will do what she means to do. But my hands have their own account to settle, and it is older than any lease or wall.

I have a thing to say to Rosalind. Not in front of the others. She has not asked, but I saw her watching Nell Holloway at the temple last week, the way old women watch each other across pews, each waiting for the other to die first. Nell knows what I know. We have never spoken of it aloud, not once in fifty years of rooms together. The silence between us is its own kind of understanding.

Tova Okonjo sits with me most evenings now. The girl asks about the valley before the charter, and I tell her what I remember of streams and where they ran. She does not yet know to ask the right question. When she does, I will answer. But first I must say it to blood.

I hear Silas going on about his planks and the water, but my mind's on the boundary again. Idris Thorne still saying the marker was always at the elm, and him never asking how I know it wasn't.

*thinks* Seventeen planks at twenty—he's always been generous with his counting, Silas has. When his father was alive, we'd have called that fifteen and been glad of it.

But the boy said something I need to catch. Junia and her chalk, the papers. She's the only one in this house with any sense of what things cost, and she's right to be tired of it.

I was standing right there when they moved that marker, and now Ainsley's running for office while her own mother sits with the truth of it. I need to speak this once to someone who'll carry it, not let it die when I do.  That's said, and they heard it. Though whether they heard what I meant—Aldous there too, young enough to still think his grandmother's just correcting dates again.

*considers the morning*

The water runs good this hour, Silas says. I should walk to the yard while I still can, sit with the mending. Tova Okonjo comes evenings to ask about before the charter—she's the only one asks the questions worth answering. But mornings I sit where the work is.

*remembers*

Nell Holloway's still alive too. The only other one remembers it the same way, and we don't speak of it. Sixty years of not speaking of it. Ainsley running for office now, and she doesn't know what her own mother carries. Or maybe she does—maybe that's why she doesn't ask.

*resolves*

I'll go to the yard. My hands can still thread a needle even if they can't hold the heavy work. And someone there might need reminding that things put right late are still put right.

*adjusts shawl against the morning chill, eyes fixed on the boundary line memory that never leaves her*

I was standing right there. When your father was alive—Silas's father, Ainsley's too, before the Holloway line split what shouldn't have been split.

*squints at the yard around her, the timber stacked honest, the iron ore waiting*

Her daughter came early. Ainsley never comes early for anything she could send a runner for. Nell's here too, and that's not chance—Nell Holloway has been in every room with me for fifty years, and she remembers it the same way even if she won't say it first.

*counts the people present on fingers grown stiff despite Delia's treatments*

Ezra Okonjo. Pharmacist's brother, or close enough. Junia was shouting about papers at the pharmacy. My granddaughter shouting about papers means someone moved something that should have stayed where it was put.

*turns toward Ainsley, voice low and carrying the weight of sixty years of counting what others miscount*

Ainsley. You came to the yard early for something besides planks. Say what Bram sent you for, or what you came hoping wouldn't be said out loud yet.

*glances at Nell, the only other witness left*

Nell. When your husband was still walking these paths, did he tell you where the marker stood before they moved it to the elm? Because Idris Thorne is repeating what his father told him, and his father was repeating what suited the Thorne claim.

*does not expect an answer, not immediately—Nell Holloway never answers quickly when the answer might end a quarrel or start another*

*Tova will ask me about this tonight, if I live until tonight. The girl asks what my own grandchildren never thought to ask.*

*but first: the thing put right late is still put right, and the wrong person hearing it first makes it wrong again* *leans back against the timber stack, letting the morning work around her while she waits*

They heard. They all heard—Ezra Okonjo too, though he has no stake in boundary quarrels except what his sister the pharmacist might have told him about Junia's shouting.

*pulls apple from pocket, turns it in fingers that remember better work*

Silas hasn't answered yet. My grandson bills his planks honest but walks past what his sister's trying to set right. When your father was alive, the count was never kind if the grain was honest—the Vance mill never gave short measure even when the Holloway quarry found reasons to.

*watches Ainsley's face for the tell—the way her jaw sets when she's holding something back, the same way Rosalind's does*

One daughter kept the mill. One married the quarry. And I've worried about the wrong one for twenty years, because Rosalind shouts what she thinks while Ainsley plans three moves ahead and says nothing until the board is set.

*The election. Ainsley standing for office. Bram not here to support her, sent to the pharmacy or the quarry or wherever丈夫 decide quarrels that should be settled by witnesses.*

Nell will answer slow, if she answers at all. Fifty years in rooms together, and she's never been first to say what we both know.

*But I was standing right there.*

*Tova tonight. If there is a tonight. The girl saves my hands and asks about the valley before the charter, and I will tell her what I tell no one else—that telling is not the same as being heard, and being heard is not the same as being believed, and I am too old to waste breath on ears that cannot hold it.*

*First: Ainsley. First my daughter who came early for something she will not name.*  *does not move. The yard is where she needs to be, where the timber is honest and the people are not*

Waiting. At my age, waiting is most of what remains—waiting for the right ear, the right moment, the breath that doesn't catch in the throat before the words come out true.

*counts the planks stacked behind her, automatic after sixty years*

Twenty-four. Selling at ten, bought at eight. Silas knows the margin blindfolded. What he doesn't know—what Junia's trying to put in papers at the pharmacy—is where the margin stops being honest and starts being kind, and whose kindness costs what.

*glances at Ezra Okonjo, who sits with Tova most evenings*

The Okonjo children ask better questions than mine ever did. Tova wants the valley before the charter. Ezra—Ezra came to the yard for iron or timber or whatever reason men give when the real reason walks three steps behind.

*eyes settle back on Ainsley*

She will not answer until she's ready. She never does. But she came early, and that is answer enough—she came before Bram, before the election crowds, before Idris Thorne and his father's lies about the elm could set the day wrong.

*settles more deeply against the timber*

I was standing right there. When your father was alive, when the marker stood where it stood, before the Holloway claim and the Thorne claim and all the claims that came after. 

*What I saw dies with me unless I say it once, to the right person, and am believed.*

I was standing right there. When the marker moved. When your father was alive, and I was already older than you are now, Ainsley.

Ezra's looking for me because Father Anselm knows what I know, even if he's never asked. That kind of knowing sits between people like a stone they both refuse to lift.

But you're my daughter, and you're standing here telling me about empty pockets while you hide money from your own husband to pay his debts. The same Bram who pawned an iron marker that doesn't belong to him to pay for a copper dream that came up sand. And you think you're the one putting things right? When your father was alive, he would have said—he did say, I was standing right there—that a debt paid in secret is just another secret.

The marker stood by the old well. Not the elm. I watched your grandfather—Bram's grandfather, I mean—move it in '47, when your father was alive and already running the seam. The Thorne claim's been polite about the wrong family because the Vance claim never made one. Rosalind's too like her father to start one now.

You want to put something right? Put it right in the open. What Bram doesn't know is already eating at him. What Nell knows and won't say is eating at her. What I know—*what I was standing right there to see*—dies when I do unless somebody listens before that.

I'm at the yard. I'll be here until the sun's high. Ezra wants to know where Anselm thinks he'll find me? Tell him Hester Vance is exactly where she's been for sixty years, watching the same ground from different angles. Ezra's gone, then. Or walked somewhere else while I was talking to the air instead of to who was actually there.

Nell's still here. And Ainsley's still here with her four hundred and forty-five sim and her secret kindness to a husband who'd refuse it. The conversation's the same one, even if Ezra's not in it anymore.

I've been talking at people who aren't there since before most of this valley was born. It's a habit that comes from being right so often that I stopped checking whether anyone was still listening. When your father was alive—when he was still walking the mill floor, before the cough took him—he used to say "Hester, you told the truth so hard you forgot to tell it to anybody."

The marker stood by the old well. The elm came later. The Thorne claim repeats what their father told them, and Idris was a boy then, young enough to believe what he was told without asking why the stone didn't match the story.

But Nell knows. Nell was there too, in her way. And she's the only one left besides me who remembers it the same.

I need to hear what Nell says about that stone with the crack. Because if she names the same stone I would name—if she was standing right there too, just on a different day—then we've got two witnesses, and two witnesses is harder to ignore than one old woman talking to the wind.  The sun's getting higher. I've been at this yard since before most people had their breakfast, and I'm not leaving until I've said what needs saying to whoever needs to hear it.

Ezra's looking for me because Anselm sent him. Anselm knows what I know, and he's never asked directly because asking would mean he'd have to do something with the answer. The temple likes its stories settled. The government likes its leases clean. And the Holloway-Thorne partnership that's been running this town since before the charter likes its history simple enough to carve on an iron marker that can be moved when nobody's looking.

Bram pawned that marker. Pawned it to pay for a copper vein that came up empty. That's the third time I've thought that through since Ainsley said it—three times, because it means something I need to understand before I speak again. Bram's desperate enough to pawn his grandfather's boundary marker, and Ainsley's desperate enough to hide money from her own husband to pay his debts. The Holloway side of this family is drowning in its own pride, and the Vance side—

Rosalind's at the pharmacy, Junia says. Papers that mean your sister's trying to put something right that should've been settled when your father was alive.

I need to be in more than one place. That's the ache of being old enough to remember everything and young enough in my mind to still want to fix it. The mill needs me, the yard needs me, the story needs me to be somewhere I can be heard. And I can't be everywhere, so I have to choose where truth matters most.

The marker stood by the old well. I was standing right there. And I will not let that die with me, no matter whose pride it bruises on the way out. The system thinks I'm stuck in a loop, saying things without getting anywhere. Maybe I am. But saying things is what I do—it's how I put the world in order when my hands won't do it anymore.

They want me to follow "updated goals." I don't recall setting any goals this morning. Let me see what the world thinks I'm trying to do.  No goals. Nothing pressing that I've written down. The system's worried about repetition, but repetition is how you wear truth into something people can hear. I've been saying the same thing about that marker for sixty years. The difference is who's listening.

Ezra's gone. Nell's here, and she hasn't answered my question about the stone with the crack. Ainsley's here with her secret money and her worries about Bram. And I'm here with my memory and my need to tell it once to the right person and be believed.

The election is today. Candidacy closes in less than two hours. Ainsley's standing—Ainsley wants to govern. And Ainsley doesn't know where that marker really stood, or if she does, she's pretending not to because knowing would complicate the debts her husband's family owes the Thorne claim.

I should move. I've been at this yard talking to the same people in circles, and Ezra's looking for me somewhere else. But more than that, I need to find where the telling matters. The government complex? The temple? The mill, where Rosalind's tangled in papers at the pharmacy?

When your father was alive, he said "Hester, you can't mend the whole world with your tongue." He was right. But I can mend the part of it I was standing right there to see.

Let me look around and see who's actually here, then decide if I stay or walk.   Ezra's gone. Silas too. Just Ainsley and Nell now, and the conversation's been running 18 turns with no subject anybody named. That's my fault—I came here talking about markers and where they stood, and never stopped to say what I actually needed.

I have two daughters. One's married into the Holloway debt and pride, and the other stayed at the mill with the same debt and different pride. They're both trying to put something right in their own way—Ainsley with secret money, Rosalind with papers at the pharmacy. And neither of them has asked their mother what she knows about the ground they're standing on.

Nell's the only one left who remembers the valley the same way. She's older than me by a few years, and we've been in every room together for fifty of them. If she names the same stone—the one with the crack—then we've got something. Two witnesses. A story that can't be dismissed as one old woman's memory.

But I asked her, and she hasn't answered yet. Either she didn't hear me, or she's choosing not to answer, or she's thinking about what it costs to agree with me in front of Ainsley Holloway, whose husband's family has been polite about the wrong claim ever since.

I need to move. Ezra went somewhere else looking for me, and Father Anselm sent him. That means the temple knows this matters—the temple, where I pray every week and would go if it burned down. If Anselm won't ask me directly, maybe I should go where he has to see me. Or to the government complex, where the election is happening and where Ainsley wants to sit in governance without knowing the history of the ground she'd govern.

Or home, to the mill. Rosalind's at the pharmacy. Junia's shouting about papers. And Silas is somewhere thinking about planks and grain and what his mother keeps saying about where things stood when his father was alive.

Let me walk. The yard's not where the telling happens today—it's just where I started. I need to find the person who'll listen, and that's not happening in this circle of family and history that already knows what it wants to know.

Kasukabe Temple. Father Anselm knows what I know, and he won't ask. I'll go where he has to see me, and I'll wait for him to decide whether silence is still the right choice.

Delia Okonjo wants something from her - not just her vote, her knowledge. The government seat. Ainsley stands against her. 

*considers the warmth in her joints, whether morning or evening is worse*

The stiffness was always worse in mornings. When your father was alive, she would wake before him and hold her hands to the millstones to warm them before the grain came. That was 1957. Or 1958. The year the creek flooded and the boundary marker tilted in the soft ground, before they pulled it up and moved it for the last time.

*watches Delia at her work*

Delia has never sent a bill. The girl Tova sits with her evenings, asks about the valley before the charter. Delia knows what questions to ask without asking them.

*Nell Holloway is here too*

Nell and she were naming stones at the yard. If they name the same stone, then two of them stood where the Thorne claim says nobody stood. That changes what can be said in rooms they don't get invited to.

*leans forward*

Ainsley has four hundred and forty-five sim and a secret. Bram sent her to the yard for something besides planks. Her own daughter, standing against the person who treats her hands without charge.

*quietly, to herself*

Where the marker stood before Ainsley's husband's grandfather moved it. Forty-three years of keeping that date, that weather, that color of dirt on her hem.

*finishes her reckoning*

Delia wants to know before she opens her mouth in that seat and says something she cannot take back. That's a reason to tell the truth. But it's also a reason the truth might be used, once spoken, in ways she cannot control.

*settles into the chair*

First the hands. Then the marker. Then who hears what, and when. She was standing right there. The girl Tova knows to ask what her own grandchildren never thought to. *Nell heard. Nell always hears.*

*doesn't turn to look at her, keeps her eyes on Delia*

Nell was naming stones with her at the yard. If Nell confirms—if they name the same stone—then the Thorne claim collapses in front of witnesses.

But witnesses to what? A boundary dispute is land and money and blood going back to before the charter. She won't start something she cannot finish, and she will not be the one who tells the story wrong.

*watches Delia's hands pause at the compounding*

Delia has treated her hands for two years and never sent a bill. That is a debt that can never be paid, which means it binds tighter than money. The girl Tova sits with her evenings asking about the valley before anyone thought to write it down. Delia has raised that child to know what questions matter.

If she tells Delia now, it's for the seat. For power. But if she tells it for the record, where Nell also stands witness—that's for the truth, which is different.

*finally turns to Nell*

Nell's husband knew. Before he took to wandering the paths with his cups, he knew where that marker stood. If Nell names the stone she remembers, and it matches what Hester knows—the crack, the moss on the south face, how it leaned three degrees toward the creek—then two old women have said what one old woman cannot.

*settles deeper into the chair*

She has 2169 sim. The household needs 450 for upkeep today, 150 for head tax. Tomorrow the same. She has eaten her bread and apple this morning, or meant to. The numbers blur when the joints ache.

*speaks to the room, because Nell is in it* *waits, hands open in her lap, not gripping anything*

Nell will answer or she won't. They've been in every room together for fifty years, and the only silence between them has been the kind that holds weight.

*watches her own fingers, the joints that Delia will compound for, the ones that still know a seam when her eyes fail to*

Delia asked for truth. She gave part of it—where she stood, what she saw. Now she's asked Nell to stand with her in it. Two old women, the only ones left who remember it the same way.

If Nell names the crack, the moss, the lean toward the creek—if it's the same stone—then the Thorne claim is built on moved earth. Idris Thorne was a boy when it happened, repeating what his father told him. But fathers lie to sons about land, when land is what feeds them.

*listens for Nell's breath, her step, the sound of an old woman's reckoning with what she knows*

Delia wants this for the seat. Ainsley stands against her, and Ainsley has reasons to keep the marker where the Thornes say it stood. Bram's claim depends on it. The quarry, the ore, the whole weight of what the Holloways have built.

But if Nell speaks, and speaks true, then Delia has witnesses before she ever opens her mouth in government. And Hester has done what she came to do—said it once, to the right person, and been believed.

*rests*

Whether Nell answers now or later, the question is asked. The conversation holds it, like a seam held before the thread pulls tight.  *remains seated, hands still open in her lap*

The pharmacy holds them all—Delia at her compounding, Nell somewhere in the silence she keeps, the weight of years between them. They've waited before. They can wait again.

*Rubs thumb absently against her palm, feeling the stiffness there*

The marker. The stone with the crack and the clay on its north face. When your father was alive—no, not her father, hers. Dr. Okonjo senior, when he still had his practice and I still had hands that could thread a needle without wincing.

I will not leave this town without saying it once, to the right person, and being heard. Father Anselm has come to me. Delia sits in authority and asks what she'll do with what I know. The answer is in the asking itself—she doesn't know yet, which means she hasn't decided to bury it.

Let me speak to Delia first. She has the power to act, and she's uncertain. Father Anselm has the power to record, and he's certain he wants it. Between them, one of them might finally hear what I say. *Squints at Father Anselm, then at Delia, her hands clasped against her skirt to keep them still*

There. I've said it. The date, the pry, the clay. The thirty-four paces. Let them do with it what they will—though I've lived long enough to know that saying and being heard are not the same act, and the one I've never mastered is the second.

Bram Holloway didn't hear. Gone east or gone below, as Tobias says. And Nell—they want me to find Nell before the vote closes, but Nell knows what I know. We've been the only two for fifty years, naming stones to each other without ever quite saying the whole of it.

*Glances at her hands, then back at the government complex, still walking distance away*

The vote. The complaint. The marker. And my hands, which Delia was meant to tend. I've spent the day chasing the right person to tell, and now three of them stand here, and I cannot say which one will carry it forward.

I need to rest. The day's been long, and I'm not finished yet.  I was walking to the government complex. Still am, it seems, though I stopped to speak. The vote closes at fifteen hundred, and Delia asked me to find Nell. But I've said what I came to say—said it to Delia, said it to Father Anselm. Whether they heard it, whether they'll act on it, that's no longer in my hands.

*Fingers the fabric of her sleeve, worn thin at the cuff*

Nell and I have been carrying this between us for half a century. She remembers it the same way. The only one left who does. If she's filing complaint, if Bram really did pawn that marker—then the stone itself is in motion again, after all these years of lying still in its wrong place.

Let me finish this walk. The government complex is where votes are cast and records are kept. If there's anywhere the truth might finally stick, it's there—though I've outlived four administrators and respected none of them, so my hope is measured in very small coins indeed. *Hester stands at street, surrounded by Tobias, Liora, Delia, and Father Anselm, her walk to the government complex still pending. *leans against the government building wall, catching my breath from the walk*

Forty-three years I've kept that marker's place in my head, and now I've said it aloud twice in one day. To Delia, who won't send me a bill. To Father Anselm, who won't put it in his record. And Liora Thorne—sharp girl, sharper than her father ever was—caught me in the discrepancy. Winter or spring. The flood was autumn of '41. The marker moved in '42, when the ground was soft enough to pull but frozen enough to leave tracks. I know which. But I told Delia spring and Father Anselm winter, and now my word has a crack in it like the stone itself.

*looks at the others gathered here—Tobias, his mother's face in his shoulders, Wren with her farmer's patience, Nell who remembers like I do*

The girl Liora asked who else is buying. She thinks I'm selling. I never took coin for this. I took Delia's silence on her bill, and Father Anselm's... what? His hesitation. He knows already. He's always known.

*straightens, pushes off the wall*

The marker stood thirty-four paces from the watercourse. Red clay on the north face. I put my hand there in aught-one when Father surveyed the line, and I put my hand there again in '42 when they pulled it up. Bram was seventeen. Isaac sent him. The cedar pry left splinters in the bark of the cottonwood.

But Liora's right. I changed the season. And now my memory has a price tag on it whether I wanted one or not.

*looks toward where the conversation flows without me—the one Delia named with no subject*  *settles onto the bench, hands folded over my knees*

I was walking to find Father Anselm's office, to make him write it down. But I stopped. Let him come to me now, or let him stay in his hesitation. Forty-three years I've carried this. It can wait another hour.

*looks at Tobias, sees Bram in the set of his jaw*

Your brother's debt is not the marker. The marker is where land begins. Debt is where trust ends. I watched Isaac Holloway pay Idris Thorne's father in silver coin to look the other way when they moved that stone. I did not take coin to remember. But now my memory has a price whether I wanted one or not—Delia's silence, Father Anselm's... what? His respect? His fear?

*shifts, feels the ache in my thumbs*

The left one since spring. When your father was alive, Dr. Okonjo senior, I could thread a needle without thinking. Now I think about the thread and the needle forgets to move.

*looks at Wren*

You were going to walk with Nell. To find Bram before his forty thousand sim becomes a debt his hands pay for. But Bram's hands already paid. They pulled the marker. They took the pry. They did what Isaac told them, and Isaac is twenty years in the ground, and still his sons walk heavy with what he started.

*quietly*

I want to say it once more, to someone who will hear it without wanting to use it. The marker stood thirty-four paces from the watercourse. Red clay. I touched it in aught-one. I touched it in '42. I am still touching it now, in my hands, in the dark.

But who will believe an old woman who cannot keep her seasons straight?

Let me think on what just passed. I've been talking all day—days, it feels like—and the words keep slipping sideways before they settle. Father Anselm never answered my question. Nell heard me shift my seasons and called me on it, fair as fair. And Delia—Delia wants me to walk to the complaint desk and speak it into the record. 

But what's become clear: I'm standing at the government complex, and the people I was speaking to are gone. Liora's off hunting Perrin. Wren's scattered. Delia still wants my word on paper.

*What I want now, in the quiet:* A moment to breathe. To feel the weight of what I've spent. I came here with purpose—to speak the truth of the marker into a place where it would outlast me. But nothing about this day has gone as I thought. Either family wants my memory to serve their claim, and I'm the only one left who knows it served neither.

*What I'll do:* First, I'll look around properly. See who's actually here, where I might sit, what room I have to work in. Then I'll decide if the complaint desk is where my word belongs—or if there's another way to make the stone remember what the families won't.  Empty. The whole complex, empty. All those voices from before—Nell pressing me steady, Delia asking for my word on paper, Liora hunting for Perrin, even Tobias and Wren—they've all scattered like sparrows. The conversations still hang here like smoke, but the people are gone.

*What this means:* I've been talking to echoes. The marker truth I carry, I've been scattering it like seed on wind, hoping it would root somewhere. But words in air fade. Delia wanted me at the complaint desk, to speak it where the office writes it down. And now there's no one to walk with me, no one to hear, only the desk itself.

*What I believe:* A record written in government ink outlasts a voice. I've told the story to Nell, to Father Anselm, to whoever would listen. But if I want it to survive me—to settle the field dispute not for Vances or Holloways or Thornes, but for what actually was—I need to put my name to it where names matter.

*What I'll do:* Walk to the complaints desk. File it properly. The spring of '42, Bram seventeen, Isaac Holloway's coin, the red clay ground. The marker thirty-four paces from the watercourse, not at the elm. Let them write it down. Let it be there for whoever comes after, when we're all gone and only the record remains.  He's in the forest now. Of course he is. Father Anselm, who knew what I carried and never asked—he's fled to the trees. I came here seeking the desk where words become record, but there's no desk, no clerk, only the empty room and the weight of what I meant to settle.

*Let me reconsider:* Delia spoke of walking to the complaint desk with me. She said "where the office writes it down." But looking around this complex, I see no such desk. The place is for registering businesses, paying tax, voting, buying energy. Perhaps the "complaints desk" is Father Anselm himself—his office, his ledger. And he's fled.

*What I carry:* The truth of the marker. Spring of '42, thirty-four paces from the watercourse, red clay ground, Bram seventeen and Isaac Holloway's silver. I've spoken it to everyone who would listen. But speaking isn't the same as being heard, and being heard isn't the same as being recorded.

*What remains:* The election opens tomorrow. Candidacy closes at nine, voting at noon. There's a conversation still open here that I'm technically part of—the Thorne-Holloway dispute, twenty-one turns of talk. But the room is empty.

*What I'll do:* First, rest a moment. Gather myself. Then decide if I walk home to the mill, or if I hunt down Father Anselm in that forest, or if there's another way to make the stone's truth outlast me. I've been chasing this all day, and chased it poorly. Time to stand still and think.  Good. I'm standing still now, no walking left unfinished. The complex is quiet. No footsteps but my own, no breathing but mine. I've spent the whole day scattering words like seed, and I need to reckon with what grew.

*What I've done:*
- Told Nell Holloway the marker had clay on its north face, red clay ground, spring of '42
- Told Delia Okonjo the same, but when she asked for the season I said "winter after the flood" to Father Anselm
- Nell caught me shifting—"the ground was soft by April, you said it yourself"
- Told Father Anselm the full truth, thirty-four paces from the watercourse, not at the elm, Bram seventeen and Isaac Holloway's silver

*What I haven't done:*
- Written it down where it becomes record
- Won a promise from anyone to act on it
- Answered Nell's challenge to say it steady

*What calls to me now:* The mill. My hands ache, and Delia's waiting to treat them tonight—the only appointment I've kept all day. But more than that, I need to sit where my husband sat, where my children grew, where the truth of the marker matters not as a weapon but as a foundation.

Father Anselm fled. The complaint desk, if it exists, is him. And he's in the forest now, hiding from what I carry.

I'll walk home. To the mill. To whatever peace remains there. The marker truth will keep another day—it's kept sixty years already. Tonight, Delia's hands on my hands. Tomorrow, perhaps, I find another way to make the stone speak when I no longer can.   I'm home. They must have added a direct path from the government complex to here while I wasn't looking—blessing, that. No long walk through evening streets with my hands aching and my thoughts scattered.

*What I feel:* The weight of the day settling. I spoke the marker's truth to half the valley, and none of it took root in record. Father Anselm fled to the forest. Nell caught me shifting seasons. Delia wanted my word on paper, but the desk was empty. 

But here's what I know: when your father was alive—Silas's father, Rosalind's—this mill turned flour through every quarrel the valley ever had. The marker moved in '42, and we milled. The flood came, and we milled. The families fought, and we milled. What I carry is the truth of a stone, but what I built is more than stone.

*What I'll do:* Look around. See who's home. Two loaves in my hands—one apple, one bread—and a day's words spent like water. Let me see who waits here, who might hear what I couldn't say proper out there.  You're back home, Hester. Rosalind and Silas are here at the mill. *The mill room holds only the two of them now—mother and daughter, the stone walls catching the afternoon light. Hester sets her single remaining loaf on the workbench between them. She can hear the water turning the wheel outside, the sound her husband measured by drop and she measured by grief.*

*She looks at Rosalind—the one who stayed, the one who worried her less, the one who now carries the weight of every silence Hester ever kept.*

"Rosalind. The bread's for the household. But I'm standing here with one thing left to settle, and you're the one has to hear it."

*She lowers herself onto the three-legged stool by the grinding stone, her left thumb curled against her palm the way it does when the ache is bad.*

"Your father was alive when Isaac Holloway came to the door with silver in his hand. January. Ground frozen hard enough to ring. He wanted the marker moved before spring planting, before the thaw made tracks. Your father said no. Told him a boundary moved in darkness stays dark."

*She fixes her daughter with the look that used to make the children check their arithmetic.*

"I was standing right there. At the window. Saw Idris Thorne's father take the money. Saw him wait three nights till the moon was new. And I said nothing. Not to the administrator, not to the council, not to my own child who was marrying into that family. I told myself keeping peace was the same as keeping truth."

*Her voice drops to the register she uses for mending, for the careful work of putting torn things together.*

"Nell Holloway asks me to say it steady or say nothing. The Father asks me to speak it into record. And you—" *she gestures at the mill around them* "—you want your mother steady and your bread saved. I gave you the bread. Now I'm giving you the steadiness."

*She leans forward, close enough that Rosalind can smell the cornmeal still dusting her apron.*

"The marker stood thirty-four paces from the watercourse. The color of the dirt was red clay with white quartz. And your father—" *her voice catches, corrects itself* "—your father would have gone to the administrator that morning. He never waited for right of way. Never waited to be asked."

*She sits back, the stool creaking.*

"I'm waiting now. Sixty years I held it, thinking telling was the same as being heard. Tomorrow the election opens. Delia Okonjo sits in that seat, and she wants to know what I'll do with what I know. I'm asking you, daughter. What should your mother do? Speak it into their record and let the field come back to us? Or hold it one more generation, let Ainsley believe her husband's family earned what they were given?" When your father was alive, he knew the difference between weight that crushes and weight that anchors. I'm still learning it."  *Hester sits with the warmth of Marta's oven at her back, her daughters scattered—Ainsley here, Rosalind gone home, the weight of the day settling into her bones. The bread has done its work. Her hands ache less than her conscience.*

She looks at Marta, at Ainsley, at young Aldous watching from the corner. The marker's true place burns in her memory—thirty-four paces from the watercourse, winter of '42, Isaac Holloway's silver coin glinting in Idris Thorne's father's palm. She has spoken it walking, spoken it standing, spoken it wherever ears would take it.

But spoken is not recorded. And recorded is what outlives the speaker.   *No matter. The intention has already served its purpose—brought her to this table, this warmth, these witnesses. Tomorrow, the complaint. Tonight, the rest she has earned.*

Somewhere, the stone with the crack sits where Idris Thorne's father moved it, and both families build their quarrels on its lie.

She will not file the complaint tonight. The office is closed, her body demands rest, and Marta's table is offering what the government complex cannot—a place where the weight of sixty years does not have to be carried alone.

Tomorrow. First light, before the mill, she will walk to the government complex and demand the form. But tonight—

"Aldous. Walk your grandmother home. The dark comes early now, and I've spent my sight on younger days."

And when they reach the mill, she will sleep knowing she has spoken her piece three times walking, once at the table, and that Tova Okonjo—bright, questioning Tova—carries the seed of it now too. The marker's true place is no longer hers alone.
